question:
Patient note:
A 54-year-old woman with class III obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea treated at home with nocturnal bilevel support, insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, and biopsy-proven non-alcoholic steato-hepatitis complicated by mild portal inflammation was discovered by work colleagues slumped over her desk shortly after the start of the morning shift at an electronics assembly plant. Witnesses reported she had been coughing intermittently for two days, appeared flushed, and complained of “smothering” dyspnoea during the pre-shift briefing but had declined to leave early because of overtime incentives. At 08:17 factory first-aid staff found her seated forward, using accessory respiratory muscles, perspiring, and responding slowly to questions yet still able to state her name; an automated external defibrillator pad set recorded sinus tachycardia at 118 beats/min and pulse oximetry of 78 % while on ambient air. Emergency medical technicians arrived seven minutes later, applied a transparent helmet interface delivering a continuous distending pressure of 12 cm H₂O and blended oxygen adjusted to 0.66, and observed saturation climb only into the mid-80s despite intact airway reflexes. They placed a single 18-gauge antecubital cannula but administered neither bronchodilators, antibiotics, intravenous fluids, nor vasoactive medication during the ten-minute transport, and no endotracheal tube or bag-mask ventilation was attempted. On stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—still receiving identical non-invasive positive pressure and before any hospital-initiated therapy—she sat upright with forearms braced on the rails, tachypnoeic at 30 breaths/min, nasal flaring evident, and able to answer in short phrases though intermittently disoriented to the calendar. Initial triage vitals obtained by oscillometric cuff read 111/69 mm Hg, heart rate 116 beats/min regular, temperature 38.3 °C tympanic, and peripheral oxygen saturation oscillating between 88 % and 89 % on the documented 66 % inspired fraction. Capillary refill was two seconds, skin warm without mottling, and jugular venous pulsation was not elevated. The airway remained patent with moist mucous membranes and audible inspiratory crackles; there was no stridor or wheeze audible outside the helmet. Within three minutes of arrival a right radial arterial catheter was seated on the first pass, and an arterial blood gas drawn while ventilation settings remained unchanged revealed pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, lactate 2.7 mmol/L, and PaO₂ 103 mm Hg on 0.66 FiO₂. Focused neurologic check, performed before any sedative, recorded eyes opening to voice, confused verbal responses, and full localisation to trapezius squeeze, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13; pupils were 3 mm bilaterally and briskly reactive, corneal and cough reflexes were preserved, and no focal asymmetry of strength was identified. Chest examination through the helmet port disclosed coarse crackles over both bases with diminished breath sounds at the right lower zone but no egophony; percussion there was dull, and transmitted voice sounds were increased. Cardiac auscultation demonstrated a tachycardic but regular rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was protuberant, soft, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant; the liver edge was palpable two fingerbreadths below the costal margin, and splenomegaly was absent. Extremities showed trace bilateral ankle oedema, scattered striae, and no petechiae or purpura; distal pulses were full. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the secondary survey returned 120 mL of clear yellow urine immediately, and the patient’s glucose-monitoring application, reviewed on her smartphone, documented voids totalling approximately 1 380 mL over the previous twenty-four hours. Laboratory specimens drawn concurrently with the arterial sample—prior to any in-house antimicrobial, corticosteroid, diuretic, or crystalloid—reported white-blood-cell count 15.2 × 10³/µL with 9 % band forms, haemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, haematocrit 39 %, and platelet count 147 000 /µL. Chemistry panel returned sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, an anion gap of 14, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.48 mg/dL compared with her last documented outpatient baseline of 1.1 mg/dL four months earlier. Total bilirubin measured 1.65 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 72 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 188 U/L, albumin 3.0 g/dL, and international normalised ratio 1.3. High-sensitivity troponin was below detection, C-reactive protein 184 mg/L, and procalcitonin 5.2 ng/mL. Portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained while she remained on the helmet system showed patchy bilateral air-space opacities worst in the right mid- and lower fields with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion; the cardiac silhouette was within normal limits and there was no mediastinal shift. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a small vigorous left ventricle, normal right-sided chamber dimensions, and an inferior vena cava 1.7 cm in diameter collapsing more than 50 % with inspiration, suggesting relative euvolaemia. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded sinus tachycardia at 112 beats/min with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischaemia. Up to the precise moment all the above physiologic and biochemical data were captured, the patient had received neither antimicrobial agents nor intravenous fluids, remained spontaneously breathing through the helmet interface providing continuous positive airway pressure, maintained the aforementioned arterial pressure without pharmacologic support, exhibited marginal thrombocytopenia and moderate conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia on a background of fatty-liver disease, demonstrated early renal impairment yet preserved daily urine volume of 1 380 mL, and displayed mild encephalopathy in the setting of suspected severe bilateral pneumonia.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
SOFA assigns 0–4 points to each of six organ systems. Using the arrival measurements:
1. Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 103/0.66 ≈ 156 mm Hg. Helmet CPAP is respiratory support, so a ratio of 100 to <200 scores 3.
2. Coagulation: platelets 147,000/µL (100,000 to <150,000) → 1.
3. Liver: bilirubin 1.65 mg/dL (1.2–1.9) → 1.
4. Cardiovascular: mean arterial pressure ≈ (111 + 2 × 69)/3 = 83 mm Hg. MAP ≥70 without vasopressors → 0.
5. Neurologic: documented GCS 13 (range 13–14) → 1.
6. Renal: creatinine 1.48 mg/dL (1.2–1.9) → 1. Urine output of 1,380 mL/day does not warrant a higher score.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 7.
Final answer: 7
